chunks.section: Polar Switch: Fast Muon Orthogonalization with Polynomial Circuits Thanks: Code is available at https://github.com/zhehangdu/polar-switch .
chunks.text: Zhehang Du Weijie Su † † thanks: University of Pennsylvania. Emails: {duz,suw}@wharton.upenn.edu . October 19, 2026

Muon, a 2024-born optimizer for language models, differs from the 2015-born spectral gradient descent [ 1 , 2 ] mainly in its fast, GPU-friendly Newton–Schulz polynomial for orthogonalizing the gradient matrix. Accordingly, a line of research proposes faster polynomial iterations for gradient orthogonalization, such as Polar Express and Gram Newton--Schulz , both built on quintic polynomials. In this paper, we introduce Polar Switch , a new approach to polynomial gradient orthogonalization. Using simple polynomial circuits, Polar Switch reaches a given high polynomial degree at a lower FLOP cost than quintic iterations. We define a circuit as a short sequence of symmetric matrix products on a few square buffers, and circuits with k k products form a restricted family of odd polynomials of degree up to 2 k + 1 + 1 2^{k+1}+1 . We choose the sequence of products in each circuit, their coefficients, and how the circuits are composed by numerically minimizing a worst-case bound on the polar approximation error. This minimization is subject to a FLOP budget that accounts for symmetric matrix multiplication kernels and a rounding constraint for numerical stability in half precision. Our two recommended Polar Switch methods have 15.5–18.7% lower runtime than Polar Express on square matrices and 8.6–16.2% lower runtime than Gram Newton--Schulz on rectangular matrices with aspect ratios 3.25, 3.5, and 8, with comparable approximation accuracy. In pretraining Modded-NanoGPT #91, Qwen3-0.6B, and Gemma 3-1B, Polar Switch reaches final validation losses similar to those of established orthogonalization methods. For years, Adam [ 3 ] and AdamW [ 4 ] have been the go-to optimizers for training large language models (LLMs) [ 5 ] . Both scale the momentum coordinatewise, without explicitly accounting for the matrix structure of the parameters. Muon [ 6 ] takes a different approach in that it uses the matrix structure of the momentum and approximates its polar factor to form the update. Studies have shown that Muon can reach the same training loss as AdamW with less computation [ 7 , 8 ] , and it has since been used to train several frontier open-weight LLMs, including Kimi K3 [ 9 ] , GLM-5 [ 10 ] , Step 3.5 Flash [ 11 ] , DeepSeek-V4 [ 12 ] , and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next [ 13 ] . This advantage comes with additional computation at each optimizer step, because Muon must approximate the polar factor. The question is therefore how to compute this approximation accurately and efficiently. Let W ∈ ℝ n × m W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} be a matrix-shaped parameter, ∇ W \nabla W its gradient, and M M its momentum matrix. Without loss of generality, let n ≤ m n\leq m , because matrices with more rows than columns are handled by transposition. With momentum coefficient μ \mu and learning rate η \eta , a simplified Muon update is M ← μ ​ M + ∇ W , W ← W − η ​ polar ⁡ ( M ) . M\leftarrow\mu M+\nabla W,\qquad W\leftarrow W-\eta\operatorname{polar}(M).

However, computing an SVD at every optimizer step is expensive for LLM training. Muon approximates the polar factor using polynomial iterations inspired by Newton–Schulz [ 6 ] . Approximating the polar factor in Muon therefore requires this composition to approximate one on the positive initial singular values.

The classical Newton–Schulz iteration uses p t ​ ( x ) = ( 3 ​ x − x 3 ) / 2 p_{t}(x)=(3x-x^{3})/2 , whose repeated application converges to one for 0 < x ≤ 1 0<x\leq 1 [ 14 ] . Muon uses Jordan’s fixed quintic p t ​ ( x ) = 3.4445 ​ x − 4.775 ​ x 3 + 2.0315 ​ x 5 p_{t}(x)=3.4445x-4.775x^{3}+2.0315x^{5} [ 6 ] . Polar Express ( PE ) uses minimax approximation to choose a different quintic polynomial at each iteration, minimizing its maximum deviation from one over the current singular value interval [ 15 ] . Jordan’s method and Polar Express differ in their coefficients, but both use quintic iterations. We therefore ask the following question: Under a fixed FLOP budget for matrix orthogonalization, do repeated quintic iterations yield the most accurate polar approximation? We answer this question negatively with Polar Switch , which replaces repeated quintic iterations with a few high-degree polynomial circuits. Each circuit is a short sequence of symmetric matrix products on a small number of square buffers. For example, the first circuit of Polar Switch 3-55 ( PS3-55 ) uses three square buffers B 1 , B 2 , B 3 ∈ ℝ n × n B_{1},B_{2},B_{3}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} , with the coefficients a τ , b τ , c τ a_{\tau},b_{\tau},c_{\tau} given in Section A.2 :

We make three contributions. (i) We introduce Polar Switch , a FLOP-efficient orthogonalization method for Muon based on high-degree polynomial circuits. (ii) We develop efficient GPU implementations of Polar Switch with two or three square buffers. Each kernel combines a matrix product and its additions before one float16 store, and we select coefficients that try to keep this half-precision computation numerically stable. (iii) Across three LLM pretraining setups, Polar Switch reaches final validation losses similar to those of established orthogonalization methods. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 presents Polar Switch , explains how we design its circuits and coefficients under a FLOP budget, and describes its GPU implementation. Section 4 compares Polar Switch with quintic baselines in LLM pretraining, runtime, and approximation accuracy. Appendix A gives the theory, the numerical search, and the coefficients of Polar Switch . Appendix B gives the detailed experimental setup for LLM pretraining and the runtime and approximation accuracy experiments.

Polynomial polar iterations [ 17 ] and matrix sign methods [ 18 , 14 ] are used in eigenvalue algorithms [ 19 , 20 ] , control, and model reduction [ 21 ] . Rational alternatives include sign iterations [ 22 ] , QR-based dynamically weighted Halley (QDWH) [ 23 ] , and Zolotarev approximants [ 24 ] . Polar iterations also have backward stability analyses [ 25 ] . Broader work covers matrix roots [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ] , fractional powers [ 31 ] , general matrix function computation [ 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 , 36 ] , and manifold retractions using projected polynomials [ 37 ] . Minimax approximation minimizes the largest error over an interval, with solutions characterized by equioscillation [ 38 ] and computed by Remez methods [ 39 ] . Related problems include polynomial sign approximation [ 40 ] , rational minimax [ 41 ] and AAA approximation [ 42 ] , and Parks–McClellan filter design [ 43 , 44 ] . Paterson–Stockmeyer [ 45 ] and related methods [ 46 ] reduce the number of matrix multiplications. Other work characterizes which polynomials can be evaluated with a fixed number of products [ 47 ] . Chebyshev acceleration [ 48 ] constructs odd polynomials with large derivatives at zero to increase small singular values more quickly. Polar Express [ 15 ] proves that greedy minimax fitting is optimal for a prescribed degree sequence, and its implementation uses quintics. Dynamic programming has also been used to select minimax compositions for homomorphic comparison under multiplication and depth constraints [ 49 ] . Polar Switch selects high-degree circuits under FLOP and buffer budgets that account for symmetric GPU kernels and adds a half-precision rounding constraint for numerical stability.

Equivalent formulas can round differently because their intermediate computations differ [ 50 ] , and small singular values are sensitive to reduced precision [ 51 ] . Mixed precision is studied in linear algebra [ 52 , 53 , 54 ] and training [ 55 , 56 ] . Gram Newton--Schulz [ 16 ] accumulates square multipliers between rectangular updates, and Dion3 [ 57 ] uses it for distributed training. AMO [ 58 ] adapts iteration counts, Dion [ 59 ] uses low-rank updates, Dion2 [ 60 ] selects rows or columns, Hierarchical Muon [ 61 ] uses tiles, and CacheMuon [ 62 ] reuses transforms. Turbo-Muon [ 63 ] uses an almost-orthogonal preconditioner for faster updates, and PRISM [ 64 ] computes matrix functions adaptively. IFNSO [ 65 ] replaces the iterations with one polynomial in selected matrix powers and learns its coefficients. A cubic Newton–Schulz schedule [ 66 ] uses ten instead of fifteen dominant matrix products and reaches a similar validation loss. MuonBP [ 67 ] , CMuon [ 68 ] , and DMuon [ 69 ] support distributed computation. Polar Switch builds on polynomial Newton–Schulz iterations with efficient GPU implementations.

Muon [ 6 ] forms matrix updates by approximately orthogonalizing matrix momentum and has been used for efficient LLM training [ 7 , 8 ] . Other optimizers use diagonal gradient statistics, as in AdaGrad [ 70 ] , or factored second moments, as in Adafactor [ 71 ] . K-FAC [ 72 ] and EKFAC [ 73 ] approximate curvature using Kronecker factors. Shampoo [ 74 ] and Distributed Shampoo [ 75 ] use matrix preconditioners, and SOAP [ 76 ] applies Adam in the eigenbasis of Shampoo’s preconditioners. Spectral descent [ 1 , 2 ] exploits singular vectors. Analyses of Muon cover finite Newton–Schulz iterations [ 77 ] , inexact polar updates [ 78 ] , modular duality [ 79 ] , norm-constrained optimization [ 80 ] , preconditioning [ 81 ] (including PolarGrad [ 82 ] and Newton–Muon [ 83 ] ), curvature [ 84 ] , stability [ 85 , 86 ] , convergence [ 87 , 88 ] , and batch size [ 89 ] . Broader spectral scaling theory addresses feature learning [ 90 ] . Extensions add symmetry constraints [ 91 ] or change the normalization [ 92 ] , the preconditioning [ 93 ] , the optimization subspace [ 94 ] , or the coordinate system [ 95 ] . Activation-Keyed Momentum (AK-Momentum) [ 96 ] introduces anisotropic momentum. DeMuon [ 97 ] addresses decentralized optimization. Applications include diffusion training [ 98 ] , low-rank adaptation with ISO-LoRA [ 99 ] , and LLM training [ 100 ] . Polar Switch changes Muon’s polar approximation by designing the polynomial circuits used to form its matrix updates.

We develop Polar Switch in three steps. First, we define polynomial circuits and how they change the singular values ( Section 3.1 ). Second, we describe how we implement each circuit on a GPU in half-precision floating point and how we try to make it numerically stable ( Section 3.2 ). Third, we state the design problem that Polar Switch uses to choose its circuits and their coefficients, and we give the resulting Polar Switch methods ( Sections 3.3 and 3.4 ).

Polar Express [ 15 , Remark 3.2] permits different polynomial degrees across iterations, but its implementation uses degree five. The remark refers to dynamic programming that chooses the best sequence of polynomial iterations under a budget on the number of multiplications [ 49 ] . If each matrix multiplication has the same cost, a nonic iteration (four multiplications) is 33% more expensive than a quintic iteration (three). However, the FLOP cost on GPUs is different from the number of matrix multiplications. With symmetric kernels, a quintic iteration costs ( 3 ​ α + 1 ) ​ n 3 (3\alpha+1)n^{3} FLOPs and a nonic iteration costs ( 3 ​ α + 2 ) ​ n 3 (3\alpha+2)n^{3} FLOPs, where α = m / n \alpha=m/n ( Proposition 3.5 ). A nonic iteration thus needs only 25% more FLOPs at α = 1 \alpha=1 , and less for rectangular matrices. Polynomial iterations of higher degree therefore need fewer FLOPs on GPUs than the multiplication count suggests. This lower cost can allow more accurate polar approximations under the same FLOP budget, and Polar Switch uses it to construct circuits of high degree.

The two outer iterations of GNS have inner depths 5 5 and 9 9 on g = 4 g=4 buffers, so they are circuits in 𝒞 5 4 \mathcal{C}_{5}^{4} and 𝒞 9 4 \mathcal{C}_{9}^{4} . Their polynomials have degrees 25 25 and 125 125 , but 5 5 and 9 9 inner iterations can reach the full degrees 65 65 and 1025 1025 in ( 5 ). The gap comes from the mixed products ( i τ ≠ j τ i_{\tau}\neq j_{\tau} ), such as B 3 ← B 1 ​ B 2 B_{3}\leftarrow B_{1}B_{2} and B 1 ← B 2 ​ B 3 B_{1}\leftarrow B_{2}B_{3} , which track the Gram matrix of the updated X X . Polar Switch does not impose full degree as a constraint when optimizing its circuits and their coefficients, but all circuits we found reach full degree. For example, when g = 2 g=2 , the alternating writes of our search ( Section 3.4 ) make each inner iteration square the output of the previous one ( i τ = j τ = w τ − 1 i_{\tau}=j_{\tau}=w_{\tau-1} ), and for g = 3 g=3 , all circuits that we found also do so, so they reach the full degree. For example, PS3-55 has inner depths 5 5 and 5 5 and degrees 65 65 and 65 65 ( Section A.2 ). This suggests the hypothesis that, for a given inner depth, the most accurate way to approximate the polar factor is to use the highest possible degree, even within the restricted family 𝒫 k g \mathcal{P}_{k}^{g} . To reach the full degree 2 k + 1 + 1 2^{k+1}+1 , the largest degree among the buffers must double at every inner iteration. Then only the output of the previous inner iteration has the largest degree, so each inner iteration must square it, and a circuit with a mixed product has a lower degree. This explains why GNS reaches a lower total degree, 25 ⋅ 125 = 3125 25\cdot 125=3125 , than PS2-55 , 65 ⋅ 65 = 4225 65\cdot 65=4225 , at a higher FLOP cost ( Table 1 ).

In Algorithm 1 , each inner iteration τ \tau runs as one GPU kernel. Each buffer holds a polynomial in X ​ X 𝖳 XX^{\mathsf{T}} ( Section 3.1 ), and polynomials in the same symmetric matrix are symmetric and commute, so each product B i τ ​ B j τ = B j τ ​ B i τ B_{i_{\tau}}B_{j_{\tau}}=B_{j_{\tau}}B_{i_{\tau}} is symmetric. A symmetric matrix multiplication kernel calculates only one triangle of such a product and copies it to the other triangle. Polar Switch extends such a kernel from the QuACK kernel library ( Appendix B ). For inner iteration τ \tau , the kernel multiplies the product by a τ a_{\tau} , adds b τ ​ B r τ b_{\tau}B_{r_{\tau}} , and adds c τ c_{\tau} to each diagonal entry in its epilogue , without allocating an identity matrix. 3 3 3 In the epilogue of a matrix multiplication kernel, additional operations, such as scaling and matrix addition, can be applied to the accumulated product before storing the result in global memory, without requiring a separate kernel launch. The kernel therefore writes each output B w τ B_{w_{\tau}} to memory once, and the additions need no separate kernels or extra matrices. This kernel explains the second and third rules of Definition 3.1 . Each entry of the product B i τ ​ B j τ B_{i_{\tau}}B_{j_{\tau}} needs a full row and a full column of the two factors, so the kernel still reads the factors while it writes the output, and the output cannot overwrite a factor ( w τ ∉ { i τ , j τ } w_{\tau}\notin\{i_{\tau},j_{\tau}\} ). Each entry of the output needs only the same entry of the addend B r τ B_{r_{\tau}} , so the output can overwrite the addend ( w τ = r τ w_{\tau}=r_{\tau} ).

The circuits of Polar Switch use g g square buffers B 1 , … , B g B_{1},\ldots,B_{g} , each containing n 2 n^{2} elements. They also use two rectangular buffers, each containing m ​ n mn elements. One holds the current matrix X X . The other holds the result of the update X ← B w k ​ X X\leftarrow B_{w_{k}}X in Algorithm 1 . The result needs a separate buffer because the multiplication still needs the entries of the current X X . Once the update is complete, the result becomes the new X X . The products of a circuit have different costs on a GPU, so we count FLOPs. We count only the leading-order FLOPs of matrix products, because they are dominant for large matrices. Let α = m / n ≥ 1 \alpha=m/n\geq 1 be the aspect ratio. A symmetric kernel halves the FLOPs of a product because it calculates only one triangle.

We now explain how Polar Switch tries to keep its half-precision computation numerically stable. Polar Switch normalizes X X in float32 and converts it to float16 . 4 4 4 Following the standard Gram Newton--Schulz implementation [ 16 ] , we normalize in float32 before converting to float16 . We use float16 rather than bfloat16 because it has 10 fraction bits instead of 7. During the iterations, X X and all buffers are stored in float16 . Each product runs on float16 Tensor Cores and accumulates in float32 . The epilogue applies the scaling by a τ a_{\tau} , the addend b τ ​ B r τ b_{\tau}B_{r_{\tau}} , and the diagonal shift c τ ​ I c_{\tau}I in float32 , and then the kernel converts the result to float16 and stores it in B w τ B_{w_{\tau}} . This avoids an additional square buffer and an intermediate float16 matrix, which reduces memory traffic and avoids an additional rounding step. The main rounding of an inner iteration is likely the float16 store of its result, which rounds each entry to the nearest float16 value. For g = 2 g=2 , our numerical search uses alternating writes. Call the two buffers A A and B B . For g = 3 g=3 , the factors and the addends have many more choices. The local search may still miss the optimal solution. Our solutions are not guaranteed to be globally optimal. The problem is nonconvex, so a local search can stop at a local optimum. Also, the rounding constraint must hold for all inputs and all rounding factors. The local search checks it only on samples, and we certify every accepted circuit by interval arithmetic, which becomes expensive as k k grows.

Each experiment run uses a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. In Section 4.1 , we compare Polar Switch with the baselines in LLM training by final validation loss and numerical stability. In Section 4.2 , we compare the runtime and the approximation accuracy. The four baselines are Jordan , PE , and PE (BF16) ( Algorithm B.1 ), and GNS ( Appendix B ). PE (BF16) uses the coefficients of PE with bfloat16 storage and products and the normalization of Algorithm B.1 . Jordan and GNS are centered at the last iteration. They multiply the output of their last iteration by a constant, so that their final interval is symmetric about one. 5 5 5 Without centering, the 5 iterations of Jordan map [ 0.001 , 1 ] [0.001,1] into [ 0.470543 , 1.202369 ] [0.470543,1.202369] , which is not symmetric about one. Thus, its updates have a smaller norm than those of the other methods. In our earlier Gemma 3-1B pretraining experiments, we used Jordan without centering, and its validation loss was higher than other methods. After we centered its final interval at one, the validation losses became similar. Appendix B gives the details of the experimental setup.

We use three LLM pretraining setups, which are Modded-NanoGPT #91 [ 102 ] , Qwen3-0.6B [ 103 ] , and Gemma 3-1B [ 104 ] . In Modded-NanoGPT #91 training, PS2-64 and PS3-64 exceeded their bounds by more than 3% on 9 and 38 of 2,683,200 matrices, and PS3-64 also on 2 of 7,637,084 matrices in Gemma 3-1B training ( Table 3 ), so we recommend inner depths of at most 5 5 . A possible reason is that the rounding model ( 6 ) does not include two effects of the float16 stores. First, the store errors are additive. Let E = float16 ​ ( A ) − A E=\texttt{float16}(A)-A be the error of storing a matrix A A in float16 . Without overflow or underflow, each entry of E E is at most 2 − 11 2^{-11} (the unit roundoff of float16 ) times the magnitude of the same entry of A A , so ∥ E ∥ 2 ≤ 2 − 11 ​ n ​ ∥ A ∥ 2 \lVert E\rVert_{2}\leq 2^{-11}\sqrt{n}\,\lVert A\rVert_{2} . For n = 2048 n=2048 and ∥ A ∥ 2 = 1 \lVert A\rVert_{2}=1 , this bound is about 0.022 0.022 , which is larger than the smallest singular value 0.001 0.001 that the circuits must amplify. With this additive error, the rounding constraint in ( 9 ) would be nearly impossible to satisfy, so the rounding model ( 6 ) uses multiplicative factors. Second, E E is in general not a polynomial in X ​ X 𝖳 XX^{\mathsf{T}} , so the buffers can stop commuting, the singular values can drift, and the singular directions can mix ( Section B.2 ). These errors can grow with the inner depth. Gram Newton--Schulz also recomputes its Gram matrix from X X after two iterations for stability [ 16 ] . We recommend PS2-55 and PS3-55 , the bold rows of Table 1 .

We introduced Polar Switch , which replaces the quintic iterations in Muon with a few polynomial circuits of high degree. We select these circuits and their coefficients under a FLOP budget, and our GPU implementations run them in float16 on two or three square buffers. In our experiments, PS2-55 and PS3-55 reduced runtime by 15.5–18.7% relative to Polar Express on square matrices and by 8.6–16.2% relative to Gram Newton--Schulz on rectangular matrices, and they gave final validation losses similar to those of established orthogonalization methods in LLM pretraining.

Problem ( 9 ) is not convex. Its constraints must hold for all inputs and all rounding factors. Thus, our local search and interval certification use much computation. They give certified feasible circuits, but these circuits are not necessarily globally optimal. The number of buffer patterns increases quickly with the number g g of square buffers and the inner depth k k . Thus, for g = 3 g=3 , we searched only three fixed schedules. For g ≥ 4 g\geq 4 , a full search is not practical. The rounding model ( 6 ) is only a scalar model of the float16 rounding. It does not include additive store errors or buffers that stop commuting. The circuits with inner depth 6 6 satisfy its constraint, but they exceeded their bounds in training ( Section 4.1 ).

Problem ( 9 ) maximizes the final lower endpoint for inputs in [ ℓ 0 , 1 ] [\ell_{0},1] . For inputs below ℓ 0 \ell_{0} , it only requires that each circuit, also under the rounding model ( 6 ), maps [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] into [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Thus, it does not control the amplification of singular values below ℓ 0 \ell_{0} , and ℓ 0 = 0.001 \ell_{0}=0.001 may not be the best choice for all models. We could add a slope objective to problem ( 9 ), so that it both reduces the approximation error on [ ℓ 0 , 1 ] [\ell_{0},1] and increases the slope p ′ ​ ( 0 ) p^{\prime}(0) of the composition p p to amplify very small singular values. This slope has been maximized for Chebyshev-type polynomials [ 48 ] . Future research could test whether this improves training. Also, problem ( 9 ) maximizes the lower endpoint ℓ T \ell_{T} of the exact polynomials and uses the rounding model ( 6 ) only in its range constraint. We could also require p ~ C t ​ ( [ ℓ t − 1 , 1 ] , 𝐯 ) ⊆ [ ℓ t , 1 ] \widetilde{p}_{C_{t}}([\ell_{t-1},1];\mathbf{v})\subseteq[\ell_{t},1] for all 𝐯 ∈ [ s ′ − 1 , s ′ ] k t + 2 \mathbf{v}\in[s^{\prime-1},s^{\prime}]^{k_{t}+2} , with a second factor s ′ ∈ [ 1 , s ] s^{\prime}\in[1,s] . For s ′ = 1 s^{\prime}=1 , this is the first constraint of ( 9 ). For s ′ > 1 s^{\prime}>1 , ℓ T \ell_{T} would also be a lower bound under the rounding model with factor s ′ s^{\prime} , but the largest ℓ T \ell_{T} would not increase as s ′ s^{\prime} increases.

The kernel for each inner iteration computes B w τ ← a τ ​ B i τ ​ B j τ + b τ ​ B r τ + c τ ​ I B_{w_{\tau}}\leftarrow a_{\tau}B_{i_{\tau}}B_{j_{\tau}}+b_{\tau}B_{r_{\tau}}+c_{\tau}I . The matrix product uses fast Tensor Cores operating in half precision, with accumulation and additions in float32 . The kernel then rounds the result to float16 before storing it. This rounding happens at every inner iteration and may be the main source of rounding error in our circuits. We could instead store the result of each inner iteration in float32 . For PS2 , two float32 square buffers use the same memory in bytes as the four float16 square buffers of GNS , without changing the FLOP count. Reducing this rounding error could allow a smaller safety factor s s . PS2 could then become more accurate and more numerically stable.

Each inner iteration of Polar Switch adds c τ ​ I c_{\tau}I . GNS keeps this identity term out of the updates that track the Gram matrix, which can make these updates more numerically stable. We could also adapt problem ( 9 ) to circuits without this term by setting c τ = 0 c_{\tau}=0 in ( 3 ) and adding the constant term only in the final update, X ← B w k ​ X + c ​ X X\leftarrow B_{w_{k}}X+cX .

In our experiments, a smaller polar factor error ( 10 ) did not give a clearly lower validation loss. Jordan has the largest polar factor error ( Figure 3 ), but after centering it gave losses similar to those of the other methods. PE (BF16) has more than 15 times the diagonal drift and directional mixing of PE ( Figure 4 ), but it also gave similar losses ( Figure 1 ). In GPT-2 training, more iterations or an exact SVD also did not decrease the final loss [ 15 , 66 ] . Thus, other properties of the update may determine training quality. Candidates are the update norm (footnote 5 ), the singular directions that the update amplifies, and postprocessing, such as in NorMuon [ 92 ] . Also, all methods use the same learning rates and weight decay, which we did not tune for each method, and the best values may differ between orthogonalization methods. Further experiments could test these effects.

Future work could replace the quintic iterations of MuonBP [ 67 ] , Hierarchical Muon [ 61 ] , and Dion3 [ 57 ] with Polar Switch circuits. Polar Switch could also refresh the cached transform in CacheMuon [ 62 ] . These combinations could reduce training time.

A candidate can violate the constraint of ( 11 ) between the points of 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} , and 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . Certification is expensive, so we certify only the best candidates on 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} , and 𝒱 \mathcal{V} .

chunks.section: Appendix B Experimental Settings and Additional Results
chunks.text: Each run uses one NVIDIA B200 GPU with PyTorch 2.14.0 and CUDA 13.0. Polar Switch , Jordan , and PE use the symmetric and rectangular matrix multiplication kernels of QuACK, from the package quack-kernels 7 7 7 https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/tree/10ce505a7ecf68e46753009bd08dcf9bd6c059ee 0.6.5. We extend their epilogue with NVIDIA’s CUTLASS 8 8 8 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/tree/098de2a652cf8f00fd70b2df54051c7eccbb855a domain-specific language (DSL) 4.8.0 to add optional diagonal shifts, through a PyTorch custom operator. QuACK requires both matrix dimensions to be at least 256 and multiples of 8. For smaller matrices, such as the 192 × 768 192\times 768 matrices of Modded-NanoGPT #91, we fall back to a Triton [ 106 ] implementation of the same method, with Triton 9 9 9 https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/tree/c01b6774b1865984607d89d89d3a10833de92037 3.8.0. GNS uses the official Gram Newton--Schulz code [ 16 ] . 10 10 10 https://github.com/Dao-AILab/gram-newton-schulz/tree/e45d0aca7083cb275c9a303220c05c4abecd9187

We use the training script of record #91 of the Modded-NanoGPT short track [ 102 ] . 13 13 13 https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/blob/bc3a0c2d640d0d73dedaef87eae26148d2e32afb/train_gpt.py The model has 11 blocks, width 768, and 6 attention heads. The original script uses FlashAttention-3, and we use FlashAttention-4 [ 107 ] 14 14 14 https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/tree/1bda8f9290cd48d030f1516f0e680cd464ef3554 to run it on the B200 GPU. We train on GPT-2-tokenized FineWeb [ 108 ] for 1,250 scheduled steps followed by 40 extension steps. NorMuon [ 92 ] updates hidden matrix weights with base learning rate 0.023 0.023 , and Adam updates the remaining parameters with base learning rate 0.008 0.008 . We retain the script’s momentum, parameter-specific learning rates, weight decay, and learning-rate schedule. All methods use seeds 0–19. Final validation loss is measured on the first 10,485,760 tokens of the GPT-2-tokenized FineWeb validation shard.

We use the Qwen3-0.6B [ 103 ] architecture with random initialization. Training uses FineWeb-Edu [ 108 ] sample-100BT , using the Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B tokenizer, for 22,889 steps of 524,288 tokens. Each step accumulates gradients over 8 microbatches of 32 sequences of length 2,048. Attention uses the fused attention kernel of cuDNN [ 109 ] ( nvidia-cudnn-frontend 1.30.0) 15 15 15 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/tree/42286a6fb8792055f3db80403350e80114ea086c , and the gated MLP uses the fused MLP kernel of QuACK. Muon updates hidden matrix weights, and AdamW updates other parameters with moment decay rates 0.9 0.9 and 0.95 0.95 . Both optimizers have weight decay 0.1 0.1 , and we clip the gradient norm at 1. The learning rate increases linearly to 0.0015 0.0015 during the first 1% of training, then follows cosine decay to 0.00015 0.00015 . Muon uses momentum 0.95 0.95 and scales each matrix update by 0.2 ​ m 0.2\sqrt{m} , where m m is the larger dimension of the matrix. Validation uses a fixed sequence of 8,388,608 held-out FineWeb-Edu tokens.

We use the Gemma 3-1B [ 104 ] architecture with random initialization. Training uses FineWeb-Edu [ 108 ] sample-100BT , using the google/gemma-3-1b-pt tokenizer, for 41,962 steps of 524,288 tokens. Each step accumulates gradients over 8 microbatches of 32 sequences of length 2,048. Attention uses the fused attention kernel of cuDNN [ 109 ] ( nvidia-cudnn-frontend 1.30.0), and the gated MLP uses the fused MLP kernel of QuACK. Muon updates hidden matrix weights, and AdamW updates other parameters with moment decay rates 0.9 0.9 and 0.95 0.95 . Both optimizers have weight decay 0.1 0.1 , and we clip the gradient norm at 1. The learning rate increases linearly to 0.0005 0.0005 during the first 1% of training, then follows cosine decay to 0.00005 0.00005 . Muon uses momentum 0.95 0.95 and scales each matrix update by 0.2 ​ m 0.2\sqrt{m} , where m m is the larger dimension of the matrix. Validation uses a fixed sequence of 8,388,608 held-out FineWeb-Edu tokens.

For each tensor shape, we time all methods in five runs. Each run starts a new Python process, uses the same input for every method, and compiles each method with torch.compile before timing. The calls of different methods are interleaved: each round calls every method once. After warm-up calls, each method has at least 30 timed calls per run for single matrices and at least 15 for batches. We time each call with CUDA events, so a runtime covers one orthogonalization call on a single matrix or on a whole batch. The runtime of a method is the median time of its calls in a run, and we report the median of these runtimes over the five runs. For a runtime ratio, we divide the time of each call by the time of the reference call in the same round, where the reference method is PE , and also GNS for rectangular inputs, and we take the same two medians. Figure 5 shows the ratios relative to PE for square (top), tall (middle), and wide (bottom) inputs, and its bars span the minimum and maximum of each ratio over the five runs.
